name: Methadone
short: Long-acting full μ agonist for opioid maintenance, usually at a clinic.
mechanism: A long-acting **full μ-opioid agonist** that fully suppresses withdrawal given orally.

facts.text: Withdrawal peaks at **72–96 h** and lasts **14+ days**: less intense but much longer than heroin.

name: Buprenorphine
short: μ partial agonist for opioid maintenance; sublingual with naloxone, implant or depot.
mechanism: A **μ-opioid partial agonist**: weaker agonist effects than full agonists, yet suppresses withdrawal, especially once mild withdrawal has begun.

facts.text: Sublingual (poor oral absorption), usually with **naloxone** to deter injection; several-day outpatient supplies; also a **6-month implant** and **1-month depot**.
Withdrawal peaks ~72 h and lasts about a week; less intense than heroin.

updates.title: X-waiver gone; weekly/monthly injection
updates.text: Since January 2023 no special DATA (“X”) waiver is needed to prescribe buprenorphine for OUD. **Brixadi**, a weekly or monthly extended-release injection, was approved May 23, 2023.

name: Fentanyl
short: Synthetic opioid ~100× morphine; drives most overdose deaths.
mechanism: A very potent synthetic **μ agonist** (~100× morphine); derivatives like carfentanil are ~10,000× morphine.

facts.text: Increasingly laced into street heroin. The book claims naloxone cannot reverse fentanyl; it can, though larger or repeated doses may be needed.

updates.title: Overdose deaths falling
updates.text: US overdose deaths fell for a third straight year to about 70,000 in 2025 (provisional), with opioid-involved deaths down about 19%; synthetic opioids still dominate.

name: Lofexidine
short: α2 agonist that eases autonomic opioid withdrawal symptoms.
mechanism: An **α2-adrenergic agonist** that reduces autonomic hyperactivity during opioid withdrawal.

facts.text: Combined with **naltrexone**, reduces both the severity and the duration of withdrawal after methadone or buprenorphine (Figures 13-20, 13-21).

name: Naltrexone
short: μ-opioid antagonist for alcohol and opioid use disorders; oral or monthly injection.
mechanism: Blocks **μ-opioid** receptors, removing the opioid-mediated reward of alcohol and opioids.
uses: **Alcohol use disorder**: fewer heavy drinking days, more abstinence
**Opioid use disorder** maintenance after detoxification (monthly injection)

facts.text: Oral or **30-day injection** (380 mg IM); the injection solves adherence but is rarely prescribed.
Added to an α2 agonist, shortens opioid withdrawal; monthly injection means one decision per 30 days and can’t be stopped impulsively.
Basis of the **Sinclair method**: taken ~1 h before drinking to extinguish the drinking habit; works best paired with use.

name: Nalmefene
short: μ-opioid antagonist approved for alcohol outside the US.
mechanism: Blocks μ-opioid receptors to blunt alcohol reward.
uses: Alcohol use disorder (outside the US); Sinclair-type extinction

facts.text: Like naltrexone, reduces the euphoria of heavy drinking; approved outside the US.

updates.title: Nalmefene nasal spray for overdose
updates.text: In May 2023 the FDA approved **Opvee**, a prescription nalmefene nasal spray for emergency treatment of opioid overdose.

name: Acamprosate
short: Taurine derivative; “artificial alcohol” that quiets withdrawal glutamate.
mechanism: A taurine derivative that blocks **mGluRs** (mGlu5, perhaps mGlu2), reducing glutamate release in alcohol withdrawal; NMDA and GABA effects are probably indirect.

name: Disulfiram
short: Makes drinking aversive by blocking acetaldehyde clearance.
mechanism: **Irreversibly** inhibits liver aldehyde dehydrogenase, so alcohol produces toxic **acetaldehyde**: an aversive, conditioning reaction.

sideEffects.e: Flushing, nausea, vomiting, hypotension with alcohol (occasionally dangerous)

facts.text: The classic alcoholism drug; adherence is the problem.

name: Alcohol (ethanol)
nbn: GABA-A PAM (δ subunit); glutamate reducer; opioid releaser
short: More GABA, less glutamate, plus opioid-driven reward.
mechanism: Hypothetically enhances GABA (blocks presynaptic **GABA-B**, PAM at **δ-subunit GABA-A** receptors), reduces glutamate (presynaptic mGluRs and VSCCs; NMDA and postsynaptic mGluRs), and acts at **μ-opioid** receptors or releases β-endorphin in the VTA, driving dopamine release.

sideEffects.via: Adaptation of GABA and glutamate systems

facts.text: About **85%** of alcoholics smoke; self-medication of psychiatric disorders is common.
Listed with topiramate as unapproved agents that may help alcoholism.
